title: 1 Samuel 20:12–23
context: In the field, Jonathan swears before the LORD to warn David of Saul’s intentions, blesses him with the hope that the LORD will be with him as he was with Saul, and asks David to show covenant kindness to him and his house forever. They renew their covenant, and Jonathan arranges a signal with arrows near the stone Ezel. The passage anticipates David’s later kindness to Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9). Both traditions read it as shared ground about covenant love and faithfulness under God.

verses.text: Jonathan said to David, “By the LORD, the God of Israel, when I have sounded out my father about this time tomorrow, or the third day, behold, if there is good toward David, won’t I then send to you and disclose it to you?
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan swears by the LORD, the God of Israel, that he will sound out his father and tell David if things are good. He invokes God as witness.

Arminian readers see a solemn, freely made promise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan’s oath frames the plan in God’s presence. He commits to full disclosure.

Reformed readers see covenant faithfulness under God. Both traditions read this as shared ground about honest promises made before the LORD, with Jonathan bearing the risk of reporting his father’s intentions.

verses.text: The LORD do so to Jonathan and more also, should it please my father to do you evil, if I don’t disclose it to you and send you away, that you may go in peace. May the LORD be with you as he has been with my father.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan calls down judgment on himself if he fails to warn David, and prays, “May the LORD be with you as he has been with my father.” He anticipates David’s future.

Arminian readers see Jonathan accepting God’s purpose with humility.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan’s blessing implies that God’s favor is passing to David. He does not resist it.

Reformed readers see Jonathan submitting to God’s choice of David. Both traditions read this as shared ground and admire Jonathan’s lack of rivalry, later expressed in 23:17.

verses.text: You shall not only show me the loving kindness of the LORD while I still live, that I not die;
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan asks David to show him the LORD’s loving kindness while he lives, that he not die. He seeks protection.

Arminian readers see covenant love sought and promised mutually. Each friend binds himself to the other.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan, the king’s son, now asks for mercy from the future king. The roles are reversing.

Reformed readers see covenant kindness rooted in God’s own steadfast love. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting how naturally Jonathan speaks of David’s future position.

verses.text: but you shall also not cut off your kindness from my house forever, no, not when the LORD has cut off every one of the enemies of David from the surface of the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan also asks David never to cut off kindness from his house, even when the LORD destroys David’s enemies. His concern reaches the next generation.

Arminian readers see covenant loyalty extending to descendants.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan looks beyond his own life. David will later honor this by caring for Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:1–7).

Reformed readers see covenant promises bearing fruit across generations. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about faithfulness to commitments over time.

verses.text: So Jonathan made a covenant with David’s house, saying, “The LORD will require it at the hand of David’s enemies.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan makes a covenant with David’s house, saying the LORD will require it at the hand of David’s enemies. The covenant now includes households.

Arminian readers see a binding agreement freely made by both families.
verses.reformedNotes:
The covenant is formal and dynastic. God is called on as its guarantor.

Reformed readers see God as the one who upholds covenant promises. Both traditions read this as shared ground, seeing the friendship now bound up with the future of both households.

verses.text: Jonathan caused David to swear again, for the love that he had for him; for he loved him as he loved his own soul.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan has David swear again, because he loved him as his own soul. The covenant is grounded in love.

Arminian readers see deep, freely given friendship. The language echoes 18:1 and 18:3.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan’s love is the motive for the renewed oath. The friendship is profound.

Reformed readers see covenant love that reflects God’s own faithful love. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground and treat the friendship with respect and without speculation beyond the text.

verses.text: Then Jonathan said to him, “Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan notes that tomorrow is the new moon, and David’s empty seat will be noticed. The plan begins.

Arminian readers see practical arrangements following the solemn promises. Faith and planning go together.
verses.reformedNotes:
The plan depends on Saul noticing David’s absence. The meal will reveal Saul’s attitude.

Reformed readers see prudence working alongside covenant faith. Both traditions read this as shared ground, recalling David’s proposal in verse 5 and preparing for the account of the feast.

verses.text: When you have stayed three days, go down quickly and come to the place where you hid yourself when this started, and remain by the stone Ezel.
verses.arminianNotes:
After three days David should go to his earlier hiding place and wait by the stone Ezel. The location is known to them both.

Arminian readers see careful coordination between friends.
verses.reformedNotes:
The stone Ezel is otherwise unknown. Its exact location cannot be identified.

Reformed readers see the plan’s precision. Both traditions read this as shared ground, and both note that the meaning of the name Ezel is uncertain, so it is best not to build interpretation on it.

verses.text: I will shoot three arrows on its side, as though I shot at a mark.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan will shoot three arrows to the side of the stone, as if practicing. The signal will look ordinary.

Arminian readers see wisdom in disguising communication under threat. The signal protects both friends.
verses.reformedNotes:
The arrows provide a cover for a secret message. No one will suspect.

Reformed readers see prudent planning in danger. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground and treat the plan as a practical measure rather than a moral example in itself.

verses.text: Behold, I will send the boy, saying, ‘Go, find the arrows!’ If I tell the boy, ‘Behold, the arrows are on this side of you. Take them;’ then come, for there is peace to you and no danger, as the LORD lives.
verses.arminianNotes:
If Jonathan tells the boy the arrows are on this side, David may come safely, as the LORD lives. The signal for peace is set.

Arminian readers see clear, simple communication that protects everyone.
verses.reformedNotes:
The words to the boy will carry a hidden meaning for David. Jonathan swears by the LORD again.

Reformed readers see trust in God surrounding a human plan. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with the oath reminding readers that the friendship rests on the LORD.

verses.text: But if I say this to the boy, ‘Behold, the arrows are beyond you,’ then go your way, for the LORD has sent you away.
verses.arminianNotes:
If Jonathan says the arrows are beyond the boy, David must go, for the LORD has sent him away. Departure would be God’s doing.

Arminian readers see Jonathan interpreting painful separation as within God’s guidance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan attributes David’s flight to the LORD’s sending. God is acknowledged even in loss.

Reformed readers see providence governing painful outcomes. Both traditions read this as shared ground, sharing the conviction that God is at work in the friends’ separation without claiming to explain how.

verses.text: Concerning the matter which you and I have spoken of, behold, the LORD is between you and me forever.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan concludes that the LORD is between them forever regarding what they have spoken. God witnesses the covenant.

Arminian readers see lasting commitment freely sealed before God. Neither friend expects the bond to end.
verses.reformedNotes:
The LORD is the guarantor of their promises. The covenant has no end date.

Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness upholding human covenants. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground, and the phrase recurs at the farewell in verse 42.
